name: Qadi Burhan al-Din
bio: Ahmed Burhan al-Din (1345-1398) was a judge, scholar and soldier who rose to rule Sivas in central Anatolia as its sultan, holding the kingdom he had made for himself by the sword until his death in 1398. He wrote verse in Arabic, Persian and Turkish.

His Turkish divan, copied in 1395-96 and preserved in a unique manuscript in the British Museum, is the oldest surviving collection of literary lyric poetry in the Turkish of Anatolia. E. J. W. Gibb, in A History of Ottoman Poetry (1900), counts him the first Western Turkish love-poet, and the first to leave the mystic circle for ghazels, quatrains and tuyughs of love, wine and the beloved. The selection here is Gibb's English rendering of his specimens.

poems.title: Thy Ruby Lips Unto the Sugar-Bale Have Wroughten Bale
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
Thy ruby lips unto the sugar-bale have wroughten bale,
And made this parrot-heart of mine in melody to wail.

I flung my heart, ah, woe is me, upon her heart's pathway;
To save the vial cast against the stone, whate'er may vail?

She bent her eyebrow-bow and notched the arrow of her eye;
It seemeth then she would yon Turks unto this battle hail.

Her tresses and her locks do burn my soul like aloes-wood,
For this her rule with whatsoe'er she may to clutch avail.

O skinker, give into her hand the brimming bowl and see
The charm and seemliness she adds unto the wine vermeil.

poems.title: O Thou, White of Chin! and O Thou, Black of Hair
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
O thou, white of chin! and O thou, black of hair!
A myriad the tangles thy dark tresses bear.

What though that the tongue of the taper be long,
Its place is the lantern through thy radiance fair.

Distraught and bewildered the soul for her locks,
It maketh the nook of her eye its repair.

Mine eyes they are Ja'fer (yea, e'en as her lips),
Huseyn and Hasan are the twain of them there.

I'll waste to a hair for her hair-waist my frame,
The Uweys-i Qaren of her path will I fare.

poems.title: How Shall I Live On, Ah, How, Afar from Thee
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
How shall I live on, ah, how, afar from thee?
Know not I what I shall do, afar from thee.

O my Liege, from forth mine eyen pour the tears;
Poor am I, as beggar low, afar from thee.

Thou wouldst have my heart, I give my life instead;
Hard I'd hurt my heart all through, afar from thee.

Sad and woeful for each hair that thou dost wear;
To a hair I'd wear me too, afar from thee.

Lo, my eyes have entered my heart's blood, alack!
Fain of my eyes' blood I go, afar from thee.

To thy life my life is joined, O beauty bright,
Like unto a veil I show, afar from thee.

Far from thee, ah, far from thee, I burn alway;
Think not I am heedless, no, afar from thee.

poems.title: See How Yon Dearest One Again on Us a Ruse Hath Played
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
See how yon dearest one again on us a ruse hath played,
To turn our tears to blood she hath her cheek with rouge o'erlaid.

Since I have seen that mouth of hers my life hath been a doubt;
Since she hath shown that waist of hers she 's turned me to a shade.

Her eyes my soul subduing, her ears my heart undoing,
Her words as honey flowing, my reason dumb have made.

Her absence I can bear not, her union I may share not,
Yon Idol's 'fore whose face doth plenilune to crescent fade.

God's grace that beauty is which she to us unlawful makes;
How is it lawful for her eyne her lover's blood to shed?

A wand'ring vagrant is the wind since playing in her hair;
Not all ungrounded are the tales that thereanent are spread.

For all that at the fire of love of her she broiled the soul,
The moisture of her lip as cooling water she purveyed.

poems.title: Is Not Her Love the Soul Within This Lifeless Frame of Me
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)

poems.title: O Fairest One! O Fairest One! O Fairest
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
O fairest one! O fairest one! O fairest!
Thy words the Stream of Life, thy love the clearest.

I drunken am, and save thy ruby liplets
Is none may heal the ill they've wroughten, dearest.

Oh what shall we? thy tresses rest them never!
What do with these that rest not, fluttering rarest?

Behind us let us cast what nothing boots us,
And let us hale the thing that boots us nearest.

poems.title: I Said: That I Thy Lip Shall Drain, May It Be
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
I said: That I thy lip shall drain, may it be?
To this my pain, assain or bane may it be?

To union winning not, I am fallen far off;
In dreams that I thy lip shall drain, may it be?

poems.title: What Hurt Were I Made Glad by Union with Thee
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
What hurt were I made glad by union with thee?
And should I win not, what lack wouldst thou see?

Wound would I my heart, yea, to shreds it tear,
Knew I thy ruby lip the salve therefor would be.

poems.title: Again for Yon Leyli Is My Heart Mejnun-Wode
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
Again for yon Leyli is my heart Mejnun-wode,
Again for yon dearling are my tears Jeyhun-flood.

May it be that her lips have torn this heart of mine?
I looked, and behold, betwixen them was there blood!

poems.title: Said I: Thy Lip! Said She: How Sweet He Speaks
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
Said I: Thy lip! Said she: How sweet he speaks!
Said I: Thy waist! Said she: How neat he speaks!
Said I: My Soul, be all a ransom for thy locks!
Said she: This lack-all! of his wealth how feat he speaks!

poems.title: Said She: Why Thine Eyen Weeping Fain Do I See
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
Said she: Why thine eyen weeping fain do I see?
And why thy heart full of pain do I see?
Said I: O Idol, 'tis for this, that thy lip
I see not always, but only now and then do I see!

poems.title: Thy Lips for My Soul the Cure or Bane Do I See
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
Thy lips for my soul the cure or bane do I see?
Thine eyes' wound the salve my heart to assain do I see:
Love's fire, the which doth burn up Either World,
Weak for my heart alone and vain do I see.

poems.title: The Heart for Thine Eyes to Fragments Torn Must Be
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
The heart for thine eyes to fragments torn must be;
The soul in thy locks distraught and lorn must be.

For him who is hapless in thy hair, the balm,
O Idol, from thy liplet born must be.

poems.title: Life for Your Loved Give! Ye Who Lovers Be
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
Life for your Loved give! ye who Lovers be!
Who seeks a Love nor gives his life, a child is he!
Though all the world be gathered on the Judgment-plain,
To me 'twill be a void so I but win to thee!

poems.title: That Which God, or Yet Time Was, Hath Writ, Shall Be
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)

poems.title: Thanks to God, 'Tis Now of Heroes Bold the Day
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
Thanks to God, 'tis now of heroes bold the day;
All the world doth view the age with sore affray.

From the land where sinks the sun to where it springs
Flies within one breath the man of Love straightway.

poems.title: That on Earth I Have No Share, Full Well I Know
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
That on earth I have no share, full well I know.
Ah, from no one but my dearling comes my woe.
Hope is leader still in Either World, for sooth
Other store than that there is not here below.

poems.title: Beauties Like to Thee Within the World Are Few
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
Beauties like to thee within the world are few;
'Coquetry' thine air the which I held for 'True.'

For the partridge-hearts there is no hawk on earth
Save thy falcon-eyne that fierce and swift pursue.

poems.title: Pity 'Twere If Aught Hid in the Heart Remain
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
Pity 'twere if aught hid in the heart remain;
Life and Death do still the self-same beaker drain.

At the wild carouse of earth is Either World
By the man of Love as but one goblet ta'en.

poems.title: All Our Works and Deeds Before the Truth Are Known
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
All our works and deeds before The Truth are known,
All the lawful and unlawful we have done.

O cupbearer, give to us the brimming bowl,
That the stain of rust from off our heart be gone.

poems.title: Youthful Charmer Like to Thee I Ne'er Did See
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
Youthful charmer like to thee I ne'er did see;
Let the soul, the world, be sacrifice for thee.

Did there reach us of thy grace one single drop,
'Fore that drop a myriad seas one drop would be.

poems.title: With That Dearling We've Made Merry All the Night
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
poems.text:
With that dearling we've made merry all the night,
With that roguish fair whose riever glances smite.

Come then, up, and let us do by her anon
What we never yet have done by any wight!

poems.title: Still the Lover's Heart Doth Burn and Burn Alway
poems.author: Qadi Burhan al-Din
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900)
